The Yuma County Library District is located in **Arizona**.

**Tucson** is Arizona's second largest city by population (Phoenix is the largest).

**Step 3: Find the wettest year in Tucson**
According to the National Weather Service Tucson office and multiple authoritative sources, **1905** was the wettest year on record for Tucson. This year holds both the coldest and wettest annual temperature/precipitation records for the city.

While there were significant flooding events in other years (such as the devastating October 1983 flood), 1905 remains the official wettest year based on annual precipitation totals at the Tucson International Airport weather station. The city experienced extreme rainfall across all months that year, with monthly records still standing for February (4.15"), March (3.88"), April (3.53"), and November (4.61").

**Answer: 1905**

The **Yuma County Library District** (YCLD) serves the population of Yuma County, Arizona. Today, the library district consists of a Main Library located in Yuma as well as 7 branch libraries, which are located in downtown Yuma, the Foothills, Somerton, San Luis, Wellton, Dateland, and Roll. The first Yuma Library, a Carnegie library, opened February 24, 1921 with 1,053 volumes and seating for 20 persons.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-1) Located in Sunset Park, the Yuma Carnegie Library underwent several expansions and renovations over the years, including a $4.2 million renovation completed in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-2) The Yuma Carnegie library still operates today as the Heritage Branch Library in downtown Yuma.
Each library features books, magazines, newspapers, reference materials, CDs, DVDs, Internet access, printing, and copying services. Programs and classes for all ages are offered throughout the year, including storytimes, summer reading, technology training and assistance, and topics of local interest.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-3)

The Library District's mission statement is "Yuma County Library District is your center for information, community enrichment, recreational reading, and lifelong learning." Its official slogan is "Your Information Connection."
The County Board of Supervisors serves as the Library District Board of Directors. The Board of Directors is the five elected members of the Yuma County Board of Supervisors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-4) They appoint the Library District Director, establish salaries, approve contracts and the annual budget, and review and approve all policies for the Library District. Since the Library District is a special taxing district, the Board of Directors has the authority to set the Library District’s tax rate.
The Board of Trustees consists of nine members who are appointed by the Yuma County Library District Board of Directors. Board of Trustee positions are honorary and without compensation. Their primary function is to promote the development and improvement of Library District services. The Trustees recommend library policies to the Yuma County Library District Board of Directors.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-5)
The Library District is primarily funded by real property taxes. It is also supported by non-profit organizations such as Friends of Yuma County Libraries, Inc. and the Yuma Library Foundation, whose purpose is to support the district through fundraising and public awareness efforts.
The Yuma County Library District celebrated its Centennial in 2021, marking 100 years of service to Yuma County[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-6)
The 80,000-square-foot (7,400 m 2) Yuma Main Library opened on May 21, 2009 and was funded by part of a $53.7 million library bond program approved by voters in 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-7)
The Main Library has four meeting rooms, a special archival collection housed in the Arizona Room, and the Yuma Nonprofit Resource Center, which is a collaboration between the Yuma County Library District, the Yuma Area Nonprofit Institute, and the Arizona Chapter of the American Association of Grant Writers.

The Main Library also houses a locally-run café, a Friends of the Libraries shop, and a Yuma Police Department Substation. As of February 2023, the Main Library also houses a Media Studio room setup for recording audio and video for podcasts, social media and the like.

## Heritage Library & Archives
[edit]
The original Carnegie library still stands at its original 1921 location and operates today as the Heritage Library. Renovated in 2009. This location is also home to a local history archive which contains multiple collections of documents and artifacts from Yuma's past.

## Dateland & Roll Libraries
[edit]
Both the Dateland and Roll Libraries were co-located inside county schools, and typically closed during part of the summer holiday when classes are not in session.
The Dateland Library was located inside Dateland Elementary School while the Roll Branch is housed inside the Mohawk Valley School.
In 2026, the district terminated their contract with both Dateland and Roll, at which time these libraries returned to being only school libraries and no longer part of the system.

The **Yuma County Library District** (YCLD) serves the population of Yuma County, Arizona. Today, the library district consists of a Main Library located in Yuma as well as 7 branch libraries, which are located in downtown Yuma, the Foothills, Somerton, San Luis, Wellton, Dateland, and Roll. The first Yuma Library, a Carnegie library, opened February 24, 1921 with 1,053 volumes and seating for 20 persons.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-1) Located in Sunset Park, the Yuma Carnegie Library underwent several expansions and renovations over the years, including a $4.2 million renovation completed in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-2) The Yuma Carnegie library still operates today as the Heritage Branch Library in downtown Yuma.
Each library features books, magazines, newspapers, reference materials, CDs, DVDs, Internet access, printing, and copying services. Programs and classes for all ages are offered throughout the year, including storytimes, summer reading, technology training and assistance, and topics of local interest.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-3)

The Library District's mission statement is "Yuma County Library District is your center for information, community enrichment, recreational reading, and lifelong learning." Its official slogan is "Your Information Connection."
The County Board of Supervisors serves as the Library District Board of Directors. The Board of Directors is the five elected members of the Yuma County Board of Supervisors.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-4) They appoint the Library District Director, establish salaries, approve contracts and the annual budget, and review and approve all policies for the Library District. Since the Library District is a special taxing district, the Board of Directors has the authority to set the Library District’s tax rate.
The Board of Trustees consists of nine members who are appointed by the Yuma County Library District Board of Directors. Board of Trustee positions are honorary and without compensation. Their primary function is to promote the development and improvement of Library District services. The Trustees recommend library policies to the Yuma County Library District Board of Directors.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-5)
The Library District is primarily funded by real property taxes. It is also supported by non-profit organizations such as Friends of Yuma County Libraries, Inc. and the Yuma Library Foundation, whose purpose is to support the district through fundraising and public awareness efforts.
The Yuma County Library District celebrated its Centennial in 2021, marking 100 years of service to Yuma County[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-6)
The 80,000-square-foot (7,400 m 2) Yuma Main Library opened on May 21, 2009 and was funded by part of a $53.7 million library bond program approved by voters in 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuma_County_Library_District#cite_note-7)
The Main Library has four meeting rooms, a special archival collection housed in the Arizona Room, and the Yuma Nonprofit Resource Center, which is a collaboration between the Yuma County Library District, the Yuma Area Nonprofit Institute, and the Arizona Chapter of the American Association of Grant Writers.

The Main Library also houses a locally-run café, a Friends of the Libraries shop, and a Yuma Police Department Substation. As of February 2023, the Main Library also houses a Media Studio room setup for recording audio and video for podcasts, social media and the like.

## Heritage Library & Archives
[edit]
The original Carnegie library still stands at its original 1921 location and operates today as the Heritage Library. Renovated in 2009. This location is also home to a local history archive which contains multiple collections of documents and artifacts from Yuma's past.

## Dateland & Roll Libraries
[edit]
Both the Dateland and Roll Libraries were co-located inside county schools, and typically closed during part of the summer holiday when classes are not in session.
The Dateland Library was located inside Dateland Elementary School while the Roll Branch is housed inside the Mohawk Valley School.
In 2026, the district terminated their contract with both Dateland and Roll, at which time these libraries returned to being only school libraries and no longer part of the system.

Rain clouds fill the sky in 2022 near Apache Junction.

## ******************************************Wherever We're Needed. We're There.******************************************

It’s been nearly two months since the monsoon season ended. But that hasn’t meant the end of rain in Phoenix this year. This week, Phoenix’s streets have been lined with wet pavements and the normally blue skies have been clouded by menacing rain clouds.
Still, it’s unlikely that this month will be among Phoenix’s wettest Novembers on record. But Phoenix will likely get enough rain to surpass its average November rainfall.
According to the National Weather Service, the city has had 0.29 inches of rain — split between Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday — so far this month. (The NWS collects its official measurements from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.) That’s about 0.3 inches away from reaching the month’s historical average of 0.59 inches. But it’s a big improvement over last year: No rain was recorded in Phoenix last November.
The current weather system, which has been traveling east from California, has mostly been concentrated in the northwest Valley on Monday and Tuesday. Parts of the northwest Valley saw as much as 2.45 inches of rain during that period, said NWS meteorologist Alicia Ryan. Some areas even saw hail.

On Wednesday and into Thursday, that rain system was more squarely concentrated on top of Sky Harbor and the East Valley. The estimated rainfall total for the storm is between 0.75 inches to one inch of rain, Ryan said on Wednesday. The East Valley was hit harder than Sky Harbor itself, according to rainfall data from the Flood Control District of Maricopa County. Some areas of the East Valley, concentrated around Mesa, saw as much as 1.26 inches of rain over that period. Only 0.17 inches of rain were measured at Sky Harbor on Wednesday.

## ******************************************Wherever We're Needed. We're There.******************************************
Data from National Weather Service

## The 10 rainiest Novembers in Phoenix history
But crack the top 10 wettest Novembers, it won’t. The November months at the top of that list all topped two inches of rain. All but one took place in the previous century. Here are the 10 wettest Novembers in Phoenix’s history:
1.   1905 – 3.61 inches of rain. Phoenix saw major destructive flooding in the Gila River basin this month.  
2.   1931 – 3.18 inches  
3.   1923 – 2.84 inches  
4.   1993 – 2.79 inches  
5.   1952 – 2.60 inches  
6.   1982 – 2.50 inches  
7.   2013 – 2.43 inches. The total rainfall this month was concentrated over a three-day period. The second day, Nov. 22, was Phoenix’s second-wettest November day on record.  
8.   1919 – 2.38 inches. The city experienced a rare snowfall this month.  
9.   1978 – 2.30 inches  
10.   1902 – 2.01 inches
So far, November 2025 has a long way to go. But it may be too early to discount this year entirely.
Last month was the third wettest October on record, with 3.26 inches of rain. It’s also possible Phoenix will experience more rain beyond Thursday. There’s a 15-30% chance of rain into the weekend and the rest of the month, with an “above normal” chance of precipitation, Ryan said.

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
**July 2026 monthly review for Tucson** **11th warmest****&15th driest on record** The July outlook from the Climate Prediction Center for Tucson favored**above**-n ormal monthly mean temperatures (39% **above** vs 28% below) and **above**-normal total precipitation amounts (40% **above**vs 27% below). The month kicked off with near-normal high temperatures of 101° & 102° and unseasonably cool low temperatures of 68° & 69°. This marked the first time since 2004 that the month opened with three consecutive sub-70° low temperatures. Above-normal high temperatures were in the 105° to 109° range from the 5th through the 10th with Excessive Heat Warnings in effect on the 7th & 8th. Moisture increase on the 7th led to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms across mostly the eastern and southern portions of the metro area. Rainfall amounts were mostly less than 0.15" with isolated spots up to 0.50". On the 8th, storms were mostly near the Catalina and Rincon mountains with isolated rainfall totals between 0.50" and 1.00" between Sabino Canyon and the Tanque Verde area. The 9th and 10th were dry. An active monsoon pattern took hold from the 11th through the 21st, delivering relief from the heat. From the 16th to the 22nd, Tucson enjoyed 7 consecutive days with high temperatures below 100°, the longest such streak in July since 2018 (which had 8). Below is a recap of the most notable days during this time period. * **11th:** Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC). Numerous severe thunderstorm warnings were issued as a line of severe thunderstorms swept across the metro area from east to west. Wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph were recorded with Davis-Monthan Air Force Base recording a wind gust of 81 mph. Rainfall was mostly less than a half an inch with localized amounts over one inch. Localized areas of flash flooding were also reported.

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
* **12th:** Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC). Another round of severe thunderstorms swept across the metro area from east to west. Wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph were recorded. Rainfall amounts were a little less than the 11th, mostly less than four-tenths, but there were localized amounts over one inch. * **13th:** Following morning light showers, scattered afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall, localized flash flooding, and isolated winds gusts up to 60 mph. * **16th:** Scattered showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rain and localized areas of flash flooding. Rainfall totals in the foothills near Sabino Canyon ranged from one to two inches. Hot temperatures returned to the area during the last 9 days of the month. Highs consistently ranged from 105° to 109° while overnight lows hovered between 80° and 84°. Extreme Heat Warnings were in effect from the 23rd to 25th, 30th, and 31st. The monthly average temperature of 89.8° ranks as the **11th warmest** July on record, tied with 2025. Temperature extremes range from a high of 109° on the 24th to a low of 68° on the 1st & 2nd. Four record warm daily low temperatures were set during the month (84° on 24th; 83° on 27th; 84° on 30th; & 83° on 31st). Rainfall totals across the Tucson metro area varied considerably, based on data from rainlog.org, CoCoRaHS, andPima County Regional Flood Control District gages. General totals range from 0.40" to 2.00" with isolated areas recording 2.50" to 4.00". At the Tucson International Airport, the official recording spot in Tucson, only 0.70" was recorded. This page lists the biggest rainstorms or snowstorms of the year in Tucson, Arizona along with the date they occurred. The information answers questions like: When was the last time more than two inches of precipitation landed on Tucson in a single day? What was the rainiest day of 2018 or a century ago?
The list gives the highest daily precipitation for each year in Tucson and the date that it happened. A date with a plus sign beside it means the same amount of moisture also fell on at least one other day earlier that year.
These records go back to 1895, with a few years missing data. During that time the heaviest downpour measured for a single day was 3.93 inches (99.8 millimetres) on July 29, 1958.
Since 1949 the precipitation extremes were observed at Tucson International Airport. Before then, the weather station was near downtown Tucson.

Jamie Donnelly
Friday night’s storms helped Tucson pass its average annual rainfall total, making it the fourth wettest year to date on record.
As of 10:50 a.m. on Saturday, Tucson reached a total of 11.79 inches of rain this year, according to the National Weather Service. The yearly normal since 1991 has been 10.61 inches.
The wettest year to date was in 1905 with a total of 15.21 inches, the National Weather Service reported.
The Tucson International Airport recorded 1.60 inches of rain from midnight to 10:50 a.m. on Saturday, the National Weather Service said. This pushed the 2021 monsoon total to 10.75 inches, making it the fourth wettest monsoon on record for Tucson.
_**Listen now and subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | RSS Feed | SoundStack | All Of Our Podcasts**_
The top wettest monsoon on record was in 1964 with a total of 13.84 inches.

# Tucson passes average annual rainfall total
The Oro Valley area received half an inch to a quarter of an inch of rainfall in the past 24 hours, the National Weather Service said. Mount Lemmon recorded 0.79 inches of rain.

Maricopa County also received significant monsoon activity. Gila Bend declared a state of emergency due to severe flooding overnight, according to the town’s Facebook page. The American Red Cross was called in to help the community and the Gila Bend Community Center opened as a temporary shelter.
The Town of Gila Bend has also requested assistance from Maricopa County and the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Department.
The National Weather Service said Tucson shouldn’t expect to see the same kind of Saturday morning storms on Sunday. The best chances for storms on Sunday will come in the afternoon. There is a 30% to 40% chance of storms throughout Sunday afternoon.
As for next week’s forecast, the beginning of the week will be fairly active and Tucson will see average monsoon activity, the National Weather Service said. After Thursday, the weather should dry out a bit and have below average thunderstorm activity.

**July 2026 monthly review for Tucson** **11th warmest****&15th driest on record** The July outlook from the Climate Prediction Center for Tucson favored**above**-n ormal monthly mean temperatures (39% **above** vs 28% below) and **above**-normal total precipitation amounts (40% **above**vs 27% below). The month kicked off with near-normal high temperatures of 101° & 102° and unseasonably cool low temperatures of 68° & 69°. This marked the first time since 2004 that the month opened with three consecutive sub-70° low temperatures. Above-normal high temperatures were in the 105° to 109° range from the 5th through the 10th with Excessive Heat Warnings in effect on the 7th & 8th. Moisture increase on the 7th led to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms across mostly the eastern and southern portions of the metro area. Rainfall amounts were mostly less than 0.15" with isolated spots up to 0.50". On the 8th, storms were mostly near the Catalina and Rincon mountains with isolated rainfall totals between 0.50" and 1.00" between Sabino Canyon and the Tanque Verde area. The 9th and 10th were dry. An active monsoon pattern took hold from the 11th through the 21st, delivering relief from the heat. From the 16th to the 22nd, Tucson enjoyed 7 consecutive days with high temperatures below 100°, the longest such streak in July since 2018 (which had 8). Below is a recap of the most notable days during this time period. * **11th:** Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC). Numerous severe thunderstorm warnings were issued as a line of severe thunderstorms swept across the metro area from east to west. Wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph were recorded with Davis-Monthan Air Force Base recording a wind gust of 81 mph. Rainfall was mostly less than a half an inch with localized amounts over one inch. Localized areas of flash flooding were also reported.

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
* **12th:** Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC). Another round of severe thunderstorms swept across the metro area from east to west. Wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph were recorded. Rainfall amounts were a little less than the 11th, mostly less than four-tenths, but there were localized amounts over one inch. * **13th:** Following morning light showers, scattered afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall, localized flash flooding, and isolated winds gusts up to 60 mph. * **16th:** Scattered showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rain and localized areas of flash flooding. Rainfall totals in the foothills near Sabino Canyon ranged from one to two inches. Hot temperatures returned to the area during the last 9 days of the month. Highs consistently ranged from 105° to 109° while overnight lows hovered between 80° and 84°. Extreme Heat Warnings were in effect from the 23rd to 25th, 30th, and 31st. The monthly average temperature of 89.8° ranks as the **11th warmest** July on record, tied with 2025. Temperature extremes range from a high of 109° on the 24th to a low of 68° on the 1st & 2nd. Four record warm daily low temperatures were set during the month (84° on 24th; 83° on 27th; 84° on 30th; & 83° on 31st). Rainfall totals across the Tucson metro area varied considerably, based on data from rainlog.org, CoCoRaHS, andPima County Regional Flood Control District gages. General totals range from 0.40" to 2.00" with isolated areas recording 2.50" to 4.00". At the Tucson International Airport, the official recording spot in Tucson, only 0.70" was recorded. This is 1.51"**below** normal and ranks as the 11th driest on record. The image below is courtesy of the Pima County Regional Flood Control District.

Friday night’s storms helped Tucson pass its average annual rainfall total, making it the fourth wettest year to date on record.
As of 10:50 a.m. on Saturday, Tucson reached a total of 11.79 inches of rain this year, according to the National Weather Service. The yearly normal since 1991 has been 10.61 inches.
The wettest year to date was in 1905 with a total of 15.21 inches, the National Weather Service reported.
The Tucson International Airport recorded 1.60 inches of rain from midnight to 10:50 a.m. on Saturday, the National Weather Service said. This pushed the 2021 monsoon total to 10.75 inches, making it the fourth wettest monsoon on record for Tucson.

Title: Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
Chunks: 4,5,6,7
# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The mercury topped 100 degrees on 82 of the 92 summer days of 1994. For the year, 99 days were recorded with high temperatures of 100 degrees or more. Records were also set for consecutive days with high temperatures of 105 degrees or more (24 days - June 23rd to July 16th, old record was 15 days in 1990 - June 17th to July 1st) and 110 degrees or more (6 days - June 24th to 29th, old record was 5 days in 1990 - June 24th to 28th). The second, third and fourth hottest days on record were recorded in the summer of 1994 (116 degrees on June 29th and 115 degrees on June 25th and 28th). Overall the summer of 1994 had 19 record highs that were set or tied...7 days came within one degree of tieing a record and four days came within two degrees of tieing a record. **3). July 26 1981** - **Flash flood kills 8 at popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson.** Eight people were killed in a flash flood at Tanque Verde Falls, a popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson, when a wall of water 15 feet high rushed down the canyon and over the 100 foot falls. This was the second of three flash flood events that occurred in this area between July 25th and 30th. This event occurred around 4 PM when the area was full of swimmers and picnickers. The other two events occurred at times when few people were in the area. **2). January 1993** - **Flood event over two week period** In a two week period the area was hit with several Pacific storm systems which produced the wettest January on record and widespread flooding across the metro area. Between four and seven inches of rain fell across the metro area and in the surrounding mountains between the 5th and 19th. Runoff from snow melt from the Santa Catalina Mountains added to the flood woes.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The floods of January 1993 were the most significant to impact Pima county since the October 1983 flood. Damage to public transportation and flood control facilities, private property and inconvenience totaled up to roughly 14 million dollars for emergency repairs and long-term improvements. Improved design and construction practices developed in response to the October 1983 flood helped to minimize the amount of damage incurred and saved lives as none were lost during the flood event. **and the Number 1 weather story to affect Tucson this century was:** **the October 1983 flood** **Prior to the flood, nearly seven inches of rain fell during August and September which saturated the soil around the metro area. The wet antecedent conditions were present when on September 30th, a weather disturbance entered Arizona at the same time a surge of moisture from Tropical Storm Octave, which was located off the central Baja California coast, moved northeast across the area. The result over the four day period was torrential rains with totals across the metro area ranging from five to nine inches, causing a very destructive flood in Tucson and southeast Arizona. Bridges in the metro area, including all spanning the Santa Cruz River except one, were damaged or partially washed away. Additional damage occurred along the watercourses located throughout the metro area. Several buildings fell into Rillito Creek due to bank erosion. Extensive damage also occurred to agriculture in Marana. Cost estimates (using 1984 dollars) to repair and mitgate flood damage were estimated at $105.7 million. Four deaths in Eastern Pima County were associated with the flood.** * * * **Honorable mention (events shown from earliest to latest)** **1905 - Coldest and wettest year on record** The yearly average temperature of 65.0 degrees still stands (tied with 1912) as the coldest year on record. The average monthly temperature for April (58.3 degrees, monthly rank 2nd), May (64.6 degrees, monthly rank 1st) and June (77.6 degrees, monthly rank 2nd) are the coldest for these months on record. The monthly precipitation records still stand for February (4.15"), March (3.88"), April (3.53") and November (4.61").

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**January 7 1913 - Coldest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury bottomed out at a very cold 6 degrees on the morning of the 7th with some low-lying areas in Tucson reporting temperatures as low as zero. **December 20-24 1914 - Heavy rains and floodingkills two and damage city weils** Most rainfall ever recorded in a five day period in December (3.85") led to overflowing of all streams and dry channels. The resulting damage was the greatest south of Tucson. The roaring Santa Cruz River nearly washed away the Congress street bridge, flooded the valley and sent stranded residents into tree tops, house tops and windmills. Two people died in the storm. The flood also caused severe damage to the city wells south of town. **September 24-25 1976 - Flash flooding and hail** Tropical moisture brought heavy thunderstorms with intermittent hail to the area that rapidly filled the normally dry washes, especially the Pantano Wash and Rillito Creek. Flooding occurred on almost 100 streets and roads throughout the city, particularly on the north and east side, where local amouts of rain ranged to 3.5". Nearly a dozen cars, some with occupants, where swept into washes on the east side. Sizes of hail ranged upward to 3/4" diameter, with some as big as golf balls. Up to 5 inches of hail covered the ground in the Mt. Lemmon area. **October 6-10 1977 - Flood event** Mositure from Tropical storm Heather brought heavy rainfall during the four day period south of Tucson. The runoff from the storm caused the Santa Cruz river to have, at that time, the highest discharge known since 1892 that resulted in severe flooding. **December 25 1987 and 1916 - White Christmas across Tucson** Up to three inches of snow blanketed the metro area in 1987. This was the first white Christmas in Tucson since 1916 when four inches fell.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**June 26 1990 - Hottest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury topped out at 117 degrees on the afternoon of the 26th setting an all-time high temperature in Tucson.

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
**February 2026 Monthly Review for Tucson** **Warmest and 27th driest****on record** Dominated by high pressure for most of the month, February set a new milestone as the **warmest** on record. The month opened with a warm stretch through the 13th, featuring highs in the 70s to lower 80s and lows ranging from the 40s to mid-50s. This was interrupted on the 13th and 14th by a Pacific system that brought light rain, breezy winds, and cooler highs in the 60s. Following a brief rebound with high temperatures into the lower 70s on the 15th and 16th, a second Pacific system kept high temperatures in the low-to-mid 60s through the 20th, along with some light rain and breezy conditions. The month concluded with a dry conditions and a significant warming trend, culminating in record-breaking highs on the 27th and 28th. The monthly average temperature of 62.6° is **6.4° above normal** and ranks as the **warmest** February on record. Temperature extremes for the month ranged from a high of 89° on the 27th & 28th to a low of 36° on the 21st. This is the 28th February on record in which the official site didn't record a low temperature of 32° or colder. Daily record temperatures were set on the 5th (**warm low**; 57°, old record 54° in 1935 & 1978), 27th (**high**; 89°, old record 88° in 1906 & 1986) and 28th (**high**; 89°, old record 85° in 1986, 1988 & 2009). Rainfall amounts varied across the metro area (per sources like rainlog.org, Pima County Regional Flood Control District, and CoCoRaHS), generally ranging from 0.10" to 0.40", with isolated totals reaching up 0.60".

The Climate Prediction Center temperature and precipitation outlooks for Tucson called for the following: * a 53% chance that the seasonal mean temperatures will be **above** normal * a 14% chance that the seasonal mean temperatures will be **below** normal * a 37% chance that the seasonal total precipitation will be **below** normal * a 30% chance that the seasonal total precipitation will be **above** normal The monthly historical breakdowns were: * **December:****Warmest** and **49th driest** on record * **January:****10th warmest** and **21st wettest** on record * **February:****Warmest** and **27th driest** on record The seasonal average temperature of 59.3° is **5.0° above** normal and goes into the record books as the **WARMEST** Winter on record, **shattering** the old record of 57.9° from the Winter of 2017-18. Temperature extremes ranged from a high of 89° on February 27th and 28th to a low of 34° on January 10th. This is the **FIRST Winter on record**, since 1894, that a freezing low temperature wasn't recorded at the official location in Tucson. There were 13 daily record temperatures set (7 for highs and 6 for warm lows), which is the most in Winter since 12 were recorded in Winter 1962-63. Rainfall amounts varied across the metro area (per sources like rainlog.org, Pima County Regional Flood Control District, and CoCoRaHS), ranging from 0.75" to 3.00", with isolated totals between 3.00" & 5.00". The Tucson International airport, the official recording location, recorded 2.29" which is nearly a third of an inch below normal and ranks as the **62nd wettest** Winter season on record. The bulk of the Winter season rain occurred in January.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The mercury topped 100 degrees on 82 of the 92 summer days of 1994. For the year, 99 days were recorded with high temperatures of 100 degrees or more. Records were also set for consecutive days with high temperatures of 105 degrees or more (24 days - June 23rd to July 16th, old record was 15 days in 1990 - June 17th to July 1st) and 110 degrees or more (6 days - June 24th to 29th, old record was 5 days in 1990 - June 24th to 28th). The second, third and fourth hottest days on record were recorded in the summer of 1994 (116 degrees on June 29th and 115 degrees on June 25th and 28th). Overall the summer of 1994 had 19 record highs that were set or tied...7 days came within one degree of tieing a record and four days came within two degrees of tieing a record. **3). July 26 1981** - **Flash flood kills 8 at popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson.** Eight people were killed in a flash flood at Tanque Verde Falls, a popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson, when a wall of water 15 feet high rushed down the canyon and over the 100 foot falls. This was the second of three flash flood events that occurred in this area between July 25th and 30th. This event occurred around 4 PM when the area was full of swimmers and picnickers. The other two events occurred at times when few people were in the area. **2). January 1993** - **Flood event over two week period** In a two week period the area was hit with several Pacific storm systems which produced the wettest January on record and widespread flooding across the metro area. Between four and seven inches of rain fell across the metro area and in the surrounding mountains between the 5th and 19th. Runoff from snow melt from the Santa Catalina Mountains added to the flood woes.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The floods of January 1993 were the most significant to impact Pima county since the October 1983 flood. Damage to public transportation and flood control facilities, private property and inconvenience totaled up to roughly 14 million dollars for emergency repairs and long-term improvements. Improved design and construction practices developed in response to the October 1983 flood helped to minimize the amount of damage incurred and saved lives as none were lost during the flood event. **and the Number 1 weather story to affect Tucson this century was:** **the October 1983 flood** **Prior to the flood, nearly seven inches of rain fell during August and September which saturated the soil around the metro area. The wet antecedent conditions were present when on September 30th, a weather disturbance entered Arizona at the same time a surge of moisture from Tropical Storm Octave, which was located off the central Baja California coast, moved northeast across the area. The result over the four day period was torrential rains with totals across the metro area ranging from five to nine inches, causing a very destructive flood in Tucson and southeast Arizona. Bridges in the metro area, including all spanning the Santa Cruz River except one, were damaged or partially washed away. Additional damage occurred along the watercourses located throughout the metro area. Several buildings fell into Rillito Creek due to bank erosion. Extensive damage also occurred to agriculture in Marana. Cost estimates (using 1984 dollars) to repair and mitgate flood damage were estimated at $105.7 million. Four deaths in Eastern Pima County were associated with the flood.** * * * **Honorable mention (events shown from earliest to latest)** **1905 - Coldest and wettest year on record** The yearly average temperature of 65.0 degrees still stands (tied with 1912) as the coldest year on record. The average monthly temperature for April (58.3 degrees, monthly rank 2nd), May (64.6 degrees, monthly rank 1st) and June (77.6 degrees, monthly rank 2nd) are the coldest for these months on record. The monthly precipitation records still stand for February (4.15"), March (3.88"), April (3.53") and November (4.61").

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**January 7 1913 - Coldest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury bottomed out at a very cold 6 degrees on the morning of the 7th with some low-lying areas in Tucson reporting temperatures as low as zero. **December 20-24 1914 - Heavy rains and floodingkills two and damage city weils** Most rainfall ever recorded in a five day period in December (3.85") led to overflowing of all streams and dry channels. The resulting damage was the greatest south of Tucson. The roaring Santa Cruz River nearly washed away the Congress street bridge, flooded the valley and sent stranded residents into tree tops, house tops and windmills. Two people died in the storm. The flood also caused severe damage to the city wells south of town. **September 24-25 1976 - Flash flooding and hail** Tropical moisture brought heavy thunderstorms with intermittent hail to the area that rapidly filled the normally dry washes, especially the Pantano Wash and Rillito Creek. Flooding occurred on almost 100 streets and roads throughout the city, particularly on the north and east side, where local amouts of rain ranged to 3.5". Nearly a dozen cars, some with occupants, where swept into washes on the east side. Sizes of hail ranged upward to 3/4" diameter, with some as big as golf balls. Up to 5 inches of hail covered the ground in the Mt. Lemmon area. **October 6-10 1977 - Flood event** Mositure from Tropical storm Heather brought heavy rainfall during the four day period south of Tucson. The runoff from the storm caused the Santa Cruz river to have, at that time, the highest discharge known since 1892 that resulted in severe flooding. **December 25 1987 and 1916 - White Christmas across Tucson** Up to three inches of snow blanketed the metro area in 1987. This was the first white Christmas in Tucson since 1916 when four inches fell.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**June 26 1990 - Hottest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury topped out at 117 degrees on the afternoon of the 26th setting an all-time high temperature in Tucson.

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
**February 2026 Monthly Review for Tucson** **Warmest and 27th driest****on record** Dominated by high pressure for most of the month, February set a new milestone as the **warmest** on record. The month opened with a warm stretch through the 13th, featuring highs in the 70s to lower 80s and lows ranging from the 40s to mid-50s. This was interrupted on the 13th and 14th by a Pacific system that brought light rain, breezy winds, and cooler highs in the 60s. Following a brief rebound with high temperatures into the lower 70s on the 15th and 16th, a second Pacific system kept high temperatures in the low-to-mid 60s through the 20th, along with some light rain and breezy conditions. The month concluded with a dry conditions and a significant warming trend, culminating in record-breaking highs on the 27th and 28th. The monthly average temperature of 62.6° is **6.4° above normal** and ranks as the **warmest** February on record. Temperature extremes for the month ranged from a high of 89° on the 27th & 28th to a low of 36° on the 21st. This is the 28th February on record in which the official site didn't record a low temperature of 32° or colder. Daily record temperatures were set on the 5th (**warm low**; 57°, old record 54° in 1935 & 1978), 27th (**high**; 89°, old record 88° in 1906 & 1986) and 28th (**high**; 89°, old record 85° in 1986, 1988 & 2009). Rainfall amounts varied across the metro area (per sources like rainlog.org, Pima County Regional Flood Control District, and CoCoRaHS), generally ranging from 0.10" to 0.40", with isolated totals reaching up 0.60".

# Tucson Monthly & Seasonal Reviews for 2026
The Tucson International airport, the official recording location, recorded 0.14" which seven-tenths of an inch below normal and ranks as the **27th driest** February on record. T he first five months of the hydrological water year, October through February, have been rather wet with 5.32" being recorded at the airport. The Climate Prediction Center temperature and precipitation outlooks for Tucson called for the following: * a 53% chance that the seasonal mean temperatures will be **above** normal * a 14% chance that the seasonal mean temperatures will be **below** normal * a 37% chance that the seasonal total precipitation will be **below** normal * a 30% chance that the seasonal total precipitation will be **above** normal The monthly historical breakdowns were: * **December:****Warmest** and **49th driest** on record * **January:****10th warmest** and **21st wettest** on record * **February:****Warmest** and **27th driest** on record The seasonal average temperature of 59.3° is **5.0° above** normal and goes into the record books as the **WARMEST** Winter on record, **shattering** the old record of 57.9° from the Winter of 2017-18. Temperature extremes ranged from a high of 89° on February 27th and 28th to a low of 34° on January 10th. This is the **FIRST Winter on record**, since 1894, that a freezing low temperature wasn't recorded at the official location in Tucson. There were 13 daily record temperatures set (7 for highs and 6 for warm lows), which is the most in Winter since 12 were recorded in Winter 1962-63. Rainfall amounts varied across the metro area (per sources like rainlog.org, Pima County Regional Flood Control District, and CoCoRaHS), ranging from 0.75" to 3.00", with isolated totals between 3.00" & 5.00". The Tucson International airport, the official recording location, recorded 2.29" which is nearly a third of an inch below normal and ranks as the **62nd wettest** Winter season on record. The bulk of the Winter season rain occurred in January.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona
Title: List of municipalities in Arizona
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Map of the United States with Arizona highlighted
Arizona municipalities
Arizona is a state located in the Western United States. According to the 2020 United States census, Arizona is the 14th most populous state with 7,151,502 inhabitants (as of the 2020 census)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-StateCensus2020-1) and the 6th largest by land area spanning 113,623.1 square miles (294,282 km 2).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-Census_2020_State_Profile-2) Arizona is divided into 15 counties and contains 92 incorporatedcities and towns. Incorporated places in Arizona are those that have been granted home rule, possessing a local government in the form of a city or town council. Most of the population is concentrated within the Phoenix metropolitan area, with a 2020 census population of 4,845,832 (67.8% of the state population).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-2020_Census_Phoenix_CCD-3)

Phoenix is the capital and largest city by population in Arizona with 1,608,139 residents,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-Phoenix-4) is ranked as the fifth most populous city in the United States, and land area spanning 517.5 mi 2 (1,340 km 2) as of the 2020 census. The smallest municipality by population and land area is Winkelman with 296 residents in 0.75 mi 2 (1.9 km 2).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-Census_2020-5) The oldest incorporated place in Arizona is Tucson which incorporated in 1877 and the most recent was the town of San Tan Valley which incorporated in September 2025.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-tusayan-6)

## Municipal incorporation
[edit]
The Arizona Constitution has, since its ratification in 1912, allowed for the creation of municipal corporations in any community with a population of 3,500 or greater.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-7) According to the Constitution, a municipal charter cannot be created by special laws or by the legislature, but rather by the communities themselves as provided by general law.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-8) The population limit specified by the constitution was lowered by state law to a minimum of population of 1,500 for most locations, and further reduced to 500 for communities located within 10 miles (16 km) of a national park or national monument.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-9) State law further restricts the incorporation of new municipalities within urbanized areas, which are defined as a specific buffer zone surrounding existing cities and towns.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-10)

## Municipal incorporation
State law allows for the incorporation of a community as either a city or a town; the only additional requirement to incorporate as a city is a minimum population of 3,000.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-11) Cities and towns in Arizona function largely in an identical manner, but cities are provided with additional powers that a town charter does not provide, limited primarily to certain powers regarding the regulation of utilities and construction within the city limits.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-12) State law allows adjoining towns to merge and it allows a city to annex a town, but it does not allow cities to merge.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-14) Additionally, a town may change its form of government to a city upon reaching the minimum population of 3,000.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-15) There are, however, large communities that have remained incorporated as a town in spite of attaining a large population; Gilbert, with 267,918 residents, remains incorporated as a town.
Twenty Arizona municipalities were incorporated before 1912, when the state was admitted to the Union. As such, these cities and towns were incorporated by means other than those stipulated by current state law and the constitution. Phoenix, for example, was incorporated in 1881 by an act of the Territorial Legislature.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-16)

## Municipal incorporation
[edit]
The Arizona Constitution has, since its ratification in 1912, allowed for the creation of municipal corporations in any community with a population of 3,500 or greater.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-7) According to the Constitution, a municipal charter cannot be created by special laws or by the legislature, but rather by the communities themselves as provided by general law.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-8) The population limit specified by the constitution was lowered by state law to a minimum of population of 1,500 for most locations, and further reduced to 500 for communities located within 10 miles (16 km) of a national park or national monument.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-9) State law further restricts the incorporation of new municipalities within urbanized areas, which are defined as a specific buffer zone surrounding existing cities and towns.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Arizona#cite_note-10)

Title: Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
Chunks: 4,5,6,7
# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The mercury topped 100 degrees on 82 of the 92 summer days of 1994. For the year, 99 days were recorded with high temperatures of 100 degrees or more. Records were also set for consecutive days with high temperatures of 105 degrees or more (24 days - June 23rd to July 16th, old record was 15 days in 1990 - June 17th to July 1st) and 110 degrees or more (6 days - June 24th to 29th, old record was 5 days in 1990 - June 24th to 28th). The second, third and fourth hottest days on record were recorded in the summer of 1994 (116 degrees on June 29th and 115 degrees on June 25th and 28th). Overall the summer of 1994 had 19 record highs that were set or tied...7 days came within one degree of tieing a record and four days came within two degrees of tieing a record. **3). July 26 1981** - **Flash flood kills 8 at popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson.** Eight people were killed in a flash flood at Tanque Verde Falls, a popular recreational spot northeast of Tucson, when a wall of water 15 feet high rushed down the canyon and over the 100 foot falls. This was the second of three flash flood events that occurred in this area between July 25th and 30th. This event occurred around 4 PM when the area was full of swimmers and picnickers. The other two events occurred at times when few people were in the area. **2). January 1993** - **Flood event over two week period** In a two week period the area was hit with several Pacific storm systems which produced the wettest January on record and widespread flooding across the metro area. Between four and seven inches of rain fell across the metro area and in the surrounding mountains between the 5th and 19th. Runoff from snow melt from the Santa Catalina Mountains added to the flood woes.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
The floods of January 1993 were the most significant to impact Pima county since the October 1983 flood. Damage to public transportation and flood control facilities, private property and inconvenience totaled up to roughly 14 million dollars for emergency repairs and long-term improvements. Improved design and construction practices developed in response to the October 1983 flood helped to minimize the amount of damage incurred and saved lives as none were lost during the flood event. **and the Number 1 weather story to affect Tucson this century was:** **the October 1983 flood** **Prior to the flood, nearly seven inches of rain fell during August and September which saturated the soil around the metro area. The wet antecedent conditions were present when on September 30th, a weather disturbance entered Arizona at the same time a surge of moisture from Tropical Storm Octave, which was located off the central Baja California coast, moved northeast across the area. The result over the four day period was torrential rains with totals across the metro area ranging from five to nine inches, causing a very destructive flood in Tucson and southeast Arizona. Bridges in the metro area, including all spanning the Santa Cruz River except one, were damaged or partially washed away. Additional damage occurred along the watercourses located throughout the metro area. Several buildings fell into Rillito Creek due to bank erosion. Extensive damage also occurred to agriculture in Marana. Cost estimates (using 1984 dollars) to repair and mitgate flood damage were estimated at $105.7 million. Four deaths in Eastern Pima County were associated with the flood.** * * * **Honorable mention (events shown from earliest to latest)** **1905 - Coldest and wettest year on record** The yearly average temperature of 65.0 degrees still stands (tied with 1912) as the coldest year on record. The average monthly temperature for April (58.3 degrees, monthly rank 2nd), May (64.6 degrees, monthly rank 1st) and June (77.6 degrees, monthly rank 2nd) are the coldest for these months on record. The monthly precipitation records still stand for February (4.15"), March (3.88"), April (3.53") and November (4.61").

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**January 7 1913 - Coldest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury bottomed out at a very cold 6 degrees on the morning of the 7th with some low-lying areas in Tucson reporting temperatures as low as zero. **December 20-24 1914 - Heavy rains and floodingkills two and damage city weils** Most rainfall ever recorded in a five day period in December (3.85") led to overflowing of all streams and dry channels. The resulting damage was the greatest south of Tucson. The roaring Santa Cruz River nearly washed away the Congress street bridge, flooded the valley and sent stranded residents into tree tops, house tops and windmills. Two people died in the storm. The flood also caused severe damage to the city wells south of town. **September 24-25 1976 - Flash flooding and hail** Tropical moisture brought heavy thunderstorms with intermittent hail to the area that rapidly filled the normally dry washes, especially the Pantano Wash and Rillito Creek. Flooding occurred on almost 100 streets and roads throughout the city, particularly on the north and east side, where local amouts of rain ranged to 3.5". Nearly a dozen cars, some with occupants, where swept into washes on the east side. Sizes of hail ranged upward to 3/4" diameter, with some as big as golf balls. Up to 5 inches of hail covered the ground in the Mt. Lemmon area. **October 6-10 1977 - Flood event** Mositure from Tropical storm Heather brought heavy rainfall during the four day period south of Tucson. The runoff from the storm caused the Santa Cruz river to have, at that time, the highest discharge known since 1892 that resulted in severe flooding. **December 25 1987 and 1916 - White Christmas across Tucson** Up to three inches of snow blanketed the metro area in 1987. This was the first white Christmas in Tucson since 1916 when four inches fell.

# Top 10 weather/water/climate stories to impact the Tucson metro area during the 20th century
**June 26 1990 - Hottest temperature officially recorded in Tucson** The mercury topped out at 117 degrees on the afternoon of the 26th setting an all-time high temperature in Tucson.

Source: https://globalfutures.asu.edu/azclimate/2023/03/09/wettest-february-in-arizona/
Title: Wettest February in Arizona?
Chunks: 0,1,2
By Erinanne Saffell, posted 3/9/2024
Reanalysis of February 1905
Spring flooding events have been devastating to Arizona. The largest flood ever measured on the Salt River near Phoenix happened February 18-26, 1891. However, February 1905 actually measured more precipitation than February 1891!
The meteorological setup for February 1905 was quite different from February 1891. The main structure in 1905 consisted of a very persistent trough of low pressure in the Pacific Ocean centered near the Baja Peninsula. The winds moving around the system brought subtropical moisture into Arizona, streaming excessive precipitation across the state. The atmospheric setup in February 1891 came from a very strong trough of low pressure from the Aleutian Low in the Gulf of Alaska.
February 1905 total monthly precipitation was much larger than average February amounts
El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events have been evaluated from sea surface temperatures since 1950, but older events prior to 1950 can be calculated with the extended Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI). According to the extended MEI, 1905 was an El Nino year; 1891 was a La Nina year (1).
Temperatures were warmer in January 1905, melting a lot of the existing snowpack. The first part of February 1905 turned colder, bringing snow to Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties. February was cloudy most of the month as three storm systems dropped record-level precipitation across Arizona. There were a total of 11 rainy days and actually 2-3 thunderstorm days in February, demonstrating strong dynamics in the atmosphere (2). The wet February of 1905 caused three flooding events along the Verde, Salt, and Gila rivers, however, none were as large as the Great Flood of February 1891.
February 1905 was larger than February 1891 total monthly precipitation

Using modern county boundaries and records back to 1895, every county except Mohave experienced its wettest February on record in 1905 (Greenlee county was established in 1909, and La Paz county was established in 1983). Statewide, this was also the wettest February for the state going back to 1895, with a statewide total of 4.44 inches, more than three times the normal amount of statewide precipitation in February (5).
The vast majority of Arizona’s long-term weather records have been verified back to 1895 (the period of record, or POR) with a a handful of weather station records extending back to the 1870s. Comparing some stations that had records going back to 1891, February 1905 still measured more precipitation across the state than was measured in February 1891, making February 1905 the wettest February on record.
_Every county except Mohave had its wettest February in 1905._

## Sources
1. NOAA Physical Science Laboratory. Extended Multivariate ENSO Index. https://psl.noaa.gov/enso/mei.ext/

2. Report for February, 1905. W. L. Moore, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Climate and Crop Service of the Weather Bureau, Arizona Section. March, 1905.

3. Destructive floods in the United States in 1905. E. C. Murphy and others, U. S. Department of the Interior, United States Geological Survey. 1906.

4. Summaries of Climatological Data by Sections. C.F. Marvin, Chief of Weather Bureau. U.S. Department of Agriculture Weather Bureau. Rocky Mountain States. 1926.

5. NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Climate at a Glance. https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/

## KEY MESSAGES
Y-axis values range from 0 to 40 nights. Annual values show year-to-year variability and range from 1.4 to 36.8 nights. Five-year values also show variability as well as an increasing trend across the entire period. Five-year values are all below the long-term average of 12.8 nights between 1930 and 1999 except for the 1980 to 1984 and 1985 to 1989 periods. Since 2000, 5-year values are all above average. The 1935 to 1939 period has the lowest 5-year value at 4.6 nights, and the 2010 to 2014, 2015 to 2019, and 2020 to 2024 periods have the highest at 23.0, 24.25, and 24.26 nights, respectively.
Figure 4 Observed Number of Very Cold Nights
**Figure 4:**Observed annual number of very cold nights (minimum temperature of 0°F or lower) for Arizona from 1930 to 2024. (Comprehensive daily station data were not available prior to 1930.) Dots show annual values. Bars show averages over 5-year periods. The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of 3.1 nights. Note that this chart represents a statewide average; however, values for individual reporting stations vary greatly because of the state’s large elevation range. The number of very cold nights has mostly been below average since the 1980s, indicative of winter warming in the region. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: GHCN-Daily.
Description
Graph of the observed annual number of very cold nights for Arizona from 1930 to 2024 as described in the caption.

## KEY MESSAGES
Y-axis values range from 0 to 16 nights. Annual values show year-to-year variability and range from 0.1 to 13.8 nights. Five-year values also show variability and are all above the long-term average of 3.1 nights between 1930 and 1979 except for the 1940 to 1944 and 1955 to 1959 periods. Since 1980, 5-year values are all below average. The 2020 to 2024 period has the lowest 5-year value at 0.9 nights, and the 1930 to 1934 period has the highest at 6.8 nights.
Statewide total annual precipitation is highly variable from year to year, ranging from a low of 6.0 inches in 1956 to a high of 22.8 inches in 1905 (Figure 5); the driest 5-year period occurred in the early 1900s and was immediately followed by the wettest 5-year period. The years since the late 1990s have been relatively dry, with 20 of the last 30 years experiencing below-average precipitation. Unlike many areas of the United States, Arizona and other southwestern states have not experienced an upward trend in the frequency of extreme precipitation events. The number of 1-inch extreme precipitation events has been variable throughout the period of record and shows no long-term trend (Figure 6). Precipitation in the form of snow plays an important role: snowpack is critical for supplying water for both agricultural and urban areas (including Phoenix and Tucson) and is vital for forest health and groundwater recharge across the entire state.
Figure 5 Observed Total Annual Precipitation
**Figure 5:**Observed total annual precipitation for Arizona from 1895 to 2024. Dots show annual values. Bars show averages over 5-year periods. The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of 12.2 inches. Total annual precipitation varies widely but has mostly been below average since the late 1990s. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: NClimDiv.
Description

## KEY MESSAGES
Graph of the total annual precipitation for Arizona from 1895 to 2024 as described in the caption.
Y-axis values range from 4 to 24 inches. Annual values show year-to-year variability and range from 6.0 to 22.8 inches. Five-year values also show variability and are below the long-term average of 12.2 inches between 1895 and 1904, all near or above average between 1905 and 1944, all below average between 1945 and 1964, and all near or above average between 1965 and 1994 except for the 1970 to 1974 period. Since 1995, 5-year values are all near or below average. The 1900 to 1904 period has the lowest 5-year value at 8.6 inches, and the 1905 to 1909 period has the highest at 16.5 inches.
Figure 6 Observed Number of 1-Inch Extreme Precipitation Events
**Figure 6:**Observed annual number of 1-inch extreme precipitation events (days with precipitation of 1 inch or more) for Arizona from 1930 to 2024. (Comprehensive daily station data were not available prior to 1930.) Dots show annual values. Bars show averages over 5-year periods. The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of about 2.1 events, indicating that a typical reporting station experiences two events per year. Note that this chart represents a statewide average; however, values for individual reporting stations vary greatly because of the state’s large elevation range. The number of 1-inch extreme precipitation events is variable and shows no long-term trend. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: GHCN-Daily.
Description
Graph of the observed annual number of 1-inch extreme precipitation events for Arizona from 1930 to 2024 as described in the caption.

## KEY MESSAGES
Y-axis values range from 0 to 6 events. Annual values show year-to-year variability and range from 0.5 to 4.8 events. Five-year values also show variability and are mostly near or below the long-term average of 2.1 events across the entire period. Exceptions include the 1980 to 1984, 1990 to 1994, and 2010 to 2014 periods, which have the highest 5-year values at 2.7, 3.1, and 2.5 events, respectively. The 1945 to 1949, 1960 to 1964, and 2020 to 2024 periods have the lowest 5-year values at 1.54, 1.49, and 1.5 events, respectively.

## KEY MESSAGES
An important feature of Arizona’s summer climate is the North American Monsoon, which is a vital source of rainfall from late June or early July to mid-September. **Precipitation during the monsoon season is highly variable from year to year** but has generally been near or below the long-term average since the early 2000s (Figure 7), although the 2010–2014 period was above average due to warmer sea surface temperatures off the Pacific coast and a very active hurricane season in 2014. **In the southernmost portion of the state, monsoon rainfall accounts for more than half of the annual precipitation and plays an important role in supporting agriculture and ecosystems.** The monsoon rains are highly beneficial but can occasionally be destructive. On September 8, 2014, extremely heavy monsoon rain associated with a decaying eastern Pacific hurricane caused significant damage and flooding around the Phoenix area. The record for single-day rainfall was broken at several stations, with reports of more than 4 inches. The 2020 monsoon season was the driest on record, with only 1.5 inches of precipitation, well below the previous record low of 2.8 inches in 2009. In 2021, by contrast, the state experienced an active monsoon season, bringing relief to drought-stricken areas such as Tucson, which recorded its seventh-wettest year on record. Some of the rainfall, however, was destructive: Maricopa County saw severe flooding in August, with two deaths and a number of rooftop rescues via helicopter.
Figure 7 Observed Total Monsoon-Season Precipitation
**Figure 7:**Observed total monsoon-season (June–September) precipitation for Arizona from 1895 to 2024. Dots show annual values. Bars show averages over 5-year periods. The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of 5.3 inches. Monsoon precipitation is highly variable from year to year. Since the early 2000s, monsoon precipitation has generally been below average, with the exception of the 2010–2014 period. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: NClimDiv.
Description

## KEY MESSAGES
Graph of the observed total monsoon-season precipitation for Arizona from 1895 to 2024 as described in the caption.
Y-axis values range from 0 to 10 inches. Annual values show year-to-year variability and range from 1.5 to 8.8 inches. Five-year values also show variability and are below the long-term average of 5.3 inches between 1895 and 1904 but are all above average between 1905 1939. Since 1940, 5-year values are mostly near or below average. One notable exception is the 1980 to 1985 period, which has the highest 5-year value at 6.5 inches. The 1900 to 1904 and 2000 to 2004 periods have the lowest 5-year values at 4.2 and 4.1 inches, respectively.

## KEY MESSAGES
The historical record indicates periodic prolonged wet and dry periods (Figure 8). **Arizona is currently experiencing an extended dry period, with widespread drought conditions persisting across much or all of the state from 2002 to 2025.** More than half of Arizona was in extreme drought (defined by the US Drought Monitor) from late 2020 into the summer of 2021. Multiyear periods of high and low precipitation can cause significant variations in reservoir supplies. The latest western US drought has resulted in record-low water levels in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. Lake Mead is a critical water resource for Arizona, as well as southern Nevada, southern California, and northern Mexico. Since reaching high levels in the late 1990s, reservoir levels have been falling, reaching a historic low in 2022. In August 2021, a federal water shortage was declared by the US Bureau of Reclamation, resulting in reduced water allocations for Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico (Figure 9). Long-term droughts also raise the risk of wildfires, already a concern for this arid state. In 2011, the Wallow Fire consumed more than 500,000 acres in eastern Arizona, making it the state’s largest wildfire on record. The state also saw active fire seasons in 2020 (with nearly a million acres burned) and 2021 (more than 500,000 acres).
Figure 8 Arizona Palmer Drought Severity Index

## KEY MESSAGES
**Figure 8:**Time series of the Palmer Drought Severity Index for Arizona from the year 1000 to 2024. Values for 1895–2024 (red) are based on measured temperature and precipitation. Values prior to 1895 (blue) are estimated from indirect measures such as tree rings. The fluctuating black line is a running 20-year average. In the modern era, the wet periods of the early 1900s and the 1980s to 1990s and the dry periods of the 1950s and 2000s are evident, with the 20-year average dropping to record-low levels in the 2000s. The extended record indicates periodic occurrences of similar prolonged wet and dry periods. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: NADAv2 and NClimDiv.
Description
Line graph of the Arizona Palmer Drought Severity Index for the years 1000 to 2024 as described in the caption.
Y-axis values are divided into dry and wet categories, ranging from 0 to negative 8 (dry) and 0 to positive 8 (wet). Annual values show variability and range from negative 6.0 to positive 6.4. Annual values for most years fall between negative 3 and positive 2, but values reaching negative 4 and positive 3 are common. The 20-year running average also shows variability, with values ranging from negative 2.2 to positive 1.9. Since the beginning of the modern era (red line), the running average is generally high in the positive range until dropping below 0 in the 1940s, then rising above 0 in the 1970s. The running average shows a downward trend since the 1990s, reaching a low of negative 1.8 in 2014.

By Erinanne Saffell, posted 3/9/2024
Reanalysis of February 1905
Spring flooding events have been devastating to Arizona. The largest flood ever measured on the Salt River near Phoenix happened February 18-26, 1891. However, February 1905 actually measured more precipitation than February 1891!
The meteorological setup for February 1905 was quite different from February 1891. The main structure in 1905 consisted of a very persistent trough of low pressure in the Pacific Ocean centered near the Baja Peninsula. The winds moving around the system brought subtropical moisture into Arizona, streaming excessive precipitation across the state. The atmospheric setup in February 1891 came from a very strong trough of low pressure from the Aleutian Low in the Gulf of Alaska.
February 1905 total monthly precipitation was much larger than average February amounts
El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events have been evaluated from sea surface temperatures since 1950, but older events prior to 1950 can be calculated with the extended Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI). According to the extended MEI, 1905 was an El Nino year; 1891 was a La Nina year (1).
Temperatures were warmer in January 1905, melting a lot of the existing snowpack. The first part of February 1905 turned colder, bringing snow to Maricopa, Pima, and Pinal counties. February was cloudy most of the month as three storm systems dropped record-level precipitation across Arizona. There were a total of 11 rainy days and actually 2-3 thunderstorm days in February, demonstrating strong dynamics in the atmosphere (2). The wet February of 1905 caused three flooding events along the Verde, Salt, and Gila rivers, however, none were as large as the Great Flood of February 1891.
February 1905 was larger than February 1891 total monthly precipitation
texts.1:
Using modern county boundaries and records back to 1895, every county except Mohave experienced its wettest February on record in 1905 (Greenlee county was established in 1909, and La Paz county was established in 1983). Statewide, this was also the wettest February for the state going back to 1895, with a statewide total of 4.44 inches, more than three times the normal amount of statewide precipitation in February (5).
The vast majority of Arizona’s long-term weather records have been verified back to 1895 (the period of record, or POR) with a a handful of weather station records extending back to the 1870s. Comparing some stations that had records going back to 1891, February 1905 still measured more precipitation across the state than was measured in February 1891, making February 1905 the wettest February on record.
_Every county except Mohave had its wettest February in 1905._

Statewide total annual precipitation is highly variable from year to year, ranging from a low of 6.0 inches in 1956 to a high of 22.8 inches in 1905 (Figure 5); the driest 5-year period occurred in the early 1900s and was immediately followed by the wettest 5-year period. The years since the late 1990s have been relatively dry, with 20 of the last 30 years experiencing below-average precipitation. Unlike many areas of the United States, Arizona and other southwestern states have not experienced an upward trend in the frequency of extreme precipitation events. The number of 1-inch extreme precipitation events has been variable throughout the period of record and shows no long-term trend (Figure 6). Precipitation in the form of snow plays an important role: snowpack is critical for supplying water for both agricultural and urban areas (including Phoenix and Tucson) and is vital for forest health and groundwater recharge across the entire state.

The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of 12.2 inches. Total annual precipitation varies widely but has mostly been below average since the late 1990s. ## KEY MESSAGES
An important feature of Arizona’s summer climate is the North American Monsoon, which is a vital source of rainfall from late June or early July to mid-September. **Precipitation during the monsoon season is highly variable from year to year** but has generally been near or below the long-term average since the early 2000s (Figure 7), although the 2010–2014 period was above average due to warmer sea surface temperatures off the Pacific coast and a very active hurricane season in 2014. **In the southernmost portion of the state, monsoon rainfall accounts for more than half of the annual precipitation and plays an important role in supporting agriculture and ecosystems.** The monsoon rains are highly beneficial but can occasionally be destructive. On September 8, 2014, extremely heavy monsoon rain associated with a decaying eastern Pacific hurricane caused significant damage and flooding around the Phoenix area. The record for single-day rainfall was broken at several stations, with reports of more than 4 inches. The 2020 monsoon season was the driest on record, with only 1.5 inches of precipitation, well below the previous record low of 2.8 inches in 2009. In 2021, by contrast, the state experienced an active monsoon season, bringing relief to drought-stricken areas such as Tucson, which recorded its seventh-wettest year on record. Some of the rainfall, however, was destructive: Maricopa County saw severe flooding in August, with two deaths and a number of rooftop rescues via helicopter.
Figure 7 Observed Total Monsoon-Season Precipitation
**Figure 7:**Observed total monsoon-season (June–September) precipitation for Arizona from 1895 to 2024. Dots show annual values. Bars show averages over 5-year periods. The horizontal black line shows the long-term (entire period) average of 5.3 inches. Monsoon precipitation is highly variable from year to year. Since the early 2000s, monsoon precipitation has generally been below average, with the exception of the 2010–2014 period. Adapted from Frankson et al. 2022. Data: NClimDiv.

## KEY MESSAGES
The historical record indicates periodic prolonged wet and dry periods (Figure 8). **Arizona is currently experiencing an extended dry period, with widespread drought conditions persisting across much or all of the state from 2002 to 2025.** More than half of Arizona was in extreme drought (defined by the US Drought Monitor) from late 2020 into the summer of 2021. Multiyear periods of high and low precipitation can cause significant variations in reservoir supplies. The latest western US drought has resulted in record-low water levels in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. Lake Mead is a critical water resource for Arizona, as well as southern Nevada, southern California, and northern Mexico. Since reaching high levels in the late 1990s, reservoir levels have been falling, reaching a historic low in 2022. In August 2021, a federal water shortage was declared by the US Bureau of Reclamation, resulting in reduced water allocations for Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico (Figure 9). Long-term droughts also raise the risk of wildfires, already a concern for this arid state. In 2011, the Wallow Fire consumed more than 500,000 acres in eastern Arizona, making it the state’s largest wildfire on record. The state also saw active fire seasons in 2020 (with nearly a million acres burned) and 2021 (more than 500,000 acres).

## KEY MESSAGES
An important feature of Arizona’s summer climate is the North American Monsoon, which is a vital source of rainfall from late June or early July to mid-September. **Precipitation during the monsoon season is highly variable from year to year** but has generally been near or below the long-term average since the early 2000s (Figure 7), although the 2010–2014 period was above average due to warmer sea surface temperatures off the Pacific coast and a very active hurricane season in 2014. **In the southernmost portion of the state, monsoon rainfall accounts for more than half of the annual precipitation and plays an important role in supporting agriculture and ecosystems.** The monsoon rains are highly beneficial but can occasionally be destructive. On September 8, 2014, extremely heavy monsoon rain associated with a decaying eastern Pacific hurricane caused significant damage and flooding around the Phoenix area. The record for single-day rainfall was broken at several stations, with reports of more than 4 inches. The 2020 monsoon season was the driest on record, with only 1.5 inches of precipitation, well below the previous record low of 2.8 inches in 2009. In 2021, by contrast, the state experienced an active monsoon season, bringing relief to drought-stricken areas such as Tucson, which recorded its seventh-wettest year on record. Some of the rainfall, however, was destructive: Maricopa County saw severe flooding in August, with two deaths and a number of rooftop rescues via helicopter.

The historical record indicates periodic prolonged wet and dry periods (Figure 8). **Arizona is currently experiencing an extended dry period, with widespread drought conditions persisting across much or all of the state from 2002 to 2025.** More than half of Arizona was in extreme drought (defined by the US Drought Monitor) from late 2020 into the summer of 2021. Multiyear periods of high and low precipitation can cause significant variations in reservoir supplies. The latest western US drought has resulted in record-low water levels in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. Lake Mead is a critical water resource for Arizona, as well as southern Nevada, southern California, and northern Mexico. Since reaching high levels in the late 1990s, reservoir levels have been falling, reaching a historic low in 2022. In August 2021, a federal water shortage was declared by the US Bureau of Reclamation, resulting in reduced water allocations for Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico (Figure 9). Long-term droughts also raise the risk of wildfires, already a concern for this arid state. In 2011, the Wallow Fire consumed more than 500,000 acres in eastern Arizona, making it the state’s largest wildfire on record. The state also saw active fire seasons in 2020 (with nearly a million acres burned) and 2021 (more than 500,000 acres).
